name: Alawa
catalog_quote: In the phonological phrase the basic stress pattern is that of a rapid build up of intensity on the first syllable, and a decay of intensity on the last one to three syllables ... Within words, the penultimate syllable tends to have slightly more stress, and within the phrase marked stress is heard on certain words, usually grammatically predictable.

new_statements.quote: 4.1.1 In two syllable stems stress always appears to be penultimate, except that in interrogatives the penultimate syllable of the word is always the one stressed. On three syllable stems stress is mostly on the penultimate syllable, though a large number is heard as having stress initial. On four syllable stems stress and secondary stress occur on the first and third syllables, it sometimes being difficult to decide which has more stress. On five syllable stems, stress tends to be heard penultimate or antipenultimate, with secondary stress on the first syllable. Word stress is marked in the examples by an acute accent, morpheme break by hyphen.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog (StressTyp2) records Alawa as fixed initial stress (penultimate stress). Sharpe's description puts word stress on the PENULTIMATE syllable of the stem (two-syllable stems 'always' penultimate; her summary 'stress could always be heard as penultimate in the word'), with initial stress only as a frequent alternative hearing on three-syllable stems, as one of two near-equal peaks on four-syllable stems, and as secondary stress on five-syllable stems. The StressTyp2 initial rule is therefore not what the primary source says; at most it reflects the p.14 phrase-intensity remark or the 3/4-syllable variants. Caveat on custody: the UQ eSpace open_url is not open (record security policy…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the stem (or the only syllable of a monosyllabic stem), and is weak: 'the penultimate syllable tends to have slightly more stress' (p.14 §2.2.0); 'I tend to hear stress within words as on the penultimate syllable of the stem of the word.. though I do not always hear it in this position' (p.34 §4.1.0). Sharpe's own conclusion (p.35): 'This does suggest that to the native speaker stress could always be heard as penultimate in the word, and the variations heard could be conditioned by phrase stress interference or by the foreign grid of the linguist, imposed on a system where the stressed syllable is not very prominent in any case.' Examples p.34: máma 'food', núļa 'he', núļa-ti 'he alone', nipa-ña 'his'; aláwal 'properly', alúbuř 'over there', balpálpi 'slowly', dudúřa 'dust', ñúřadi 'right up'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Four-syllable stems: 'stress and secondary stress occur on the first and third syllables, it sometimes being difficult to decide which has more stress'; five-syllable stems: 'secondary stress on the first syllable' (p.34 §4.1.1). Mingograph curves 'show stress to be reasonably prominent on all such syllables (see Appendix K)' (p.35).
new_statements.exceptions: Interrogatives: 'the penultimate syllable of the word is always the one stressed', with a marked pitch rise (§4.1.1, §4.1.3). Three-syllable stems: 'a large number is heard as having stress initial'. Reduplicated stems (§4.1.2): stress 'normally penultimate. However if the word contains a repeated stem part, stress may be on the first syllable of the repeated part': mugululpiña 'white currant', tatpatpulúgan 'grasshopper', yililiţilili 'green parrot'. Phrase stress 'is very much more prominent than word stress' and 'can obscure this word stress' (§4.1.0, §4.2.0); phrase-level intensity shows 'rapid build up of intensity on the first syllable, and a decay of intensity on the last one to three syllables' (p.14 §2.2.0).
new_statements.identity_note: Sharpe's data are Alawa of the Hodgson Downs, Nutwood Downs and Tanumbirini stations south of the Roper River (UQ abstract), from four field trips June 1966 to May 1968; no dialect split is stated. The quoted text is from the 1972 AIAS publication (Australian Aboriginal Studies 37) of the 1970 UQ thesis; same work, different pagination.

readall_conflicts: The catalog's StressTyp2 record gives Alawa fixed initial stress; the only primary description, Sharpe's thesis as published in 1972, says word stress is (weakly) penultimate on the stem: two-syllable stems 'always' penultimate, three-syllable stems 'mostly on the penultimate syllable, though a large number is heard as having stress initial', four-syllable stems with primary and secondary on the first and third syllables 'it sometimes being difficult to decide which has more stress', five-syllable stems penultimate or antepenultimate with secondary on the first syllable, and the author's own conclusion that 'to the native speaker stress could always be heard as penultimate in the word'. So the source and the catalog disagree on placement (penultimate vs initial). Within Sharpe there is also an internal tension she flags herself: the stressed syllable 'is not very prominent in any case', phrase stress can obscure it, and Mingograph curves show comparable prominence on all the candidate syllables of longer stems; the p.14 remark about 'rapid build up of intensity on the first syllable' is about the phonological phrase, not the word.

audit.recode_to: Probably fixed-dominant (penult, stem domain) rather than fixed-strict, pending a full read of Sharpe 1972 pp.34-35: her own text (confirmed in snippets) says word stress is weak and often obscured by phrase stress, is heard on the penult 'of the stem' with variation, that 4-syllable stems carry stresses on 1st and 3rd with the primary hard to pick, and that reduplicated stems are an exception; this search of works with stress in the title's own read_rule note records 3-syllable stems 'a large number heard as having stress initial' and 5-syllable stems penult or antepenult with initial secondary. 'Strict penult at all lengths, no secondary' overstates this.
